stem: A 34-year-old man stays apneic for 3 hours after a short operation and needs ventilation. His brother had the same problem after surgery. His plasma cholinesterase activity is very low.
oneliner: 34M + 3 h of apnea after a short operation + brother had the same + very low plasma cholinesterase → which drug?
ask: Which drug given during anesthesia most likely caused this?

whyNot.B: Cleared by the **liver**, reversed with sugammadex; not plasma cholinesterase
whyNot.C: Inhaled gas; its danger is **malignant hyperthermia**, not long apnea
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepine; cleared by **CYP3A4** in the liver
whyNot.E: Opioid; cleared by **CYP3A4**, reversed by naloxone

why: **Prolonged apnea after anesthesia + low plasma cholinesterase + affected brother** = inherited pseudocholinesterase deficiency, which cannot break down **succinylcholine**.

drug.name: Succinylcholine
drug.how: Acts like acetylcholine at the nicotinic receptor and keeps the end plate depolarized
drug.watch: Hyperkalemia (burns, crush, denervation), malignant hyperthermia, prolonged block with pseudocholinesterase deficiency

stem: A 72-year-old man has constant dribbling of urine and a sense of incomplete emptying for 1 week. He takes hydrochlorothiazide, metoprolol, magnesium hydroxide, insulin glargine, and diphenhydramine at bedtime, the last started 10 days ago for sleep. Suprapubic fullness is noted, and bladder scan shows 520 mL after voiding. Glucose control is stable.
oneliner: 72M + 1 wk dribbling, incomplete emptying + 520 mL residual + HCTZ, metoprolol, Mg hydroxide, insulin, bedtime diphenhydramine started 10 d ago → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of his urinary symptoms?

whyNot.A: **Thiazide**: causes urine volume and urgency, not retention
whyNot.C: **Beta-1 selective blocker**: bradycardia and fatigue; no antimuscarinic effect
whyNot.D: **Laxative**: diarrhea; no effect on detrusor contraction
whyNot.E: **Insulin**: hypoglycemia; glucose is stable and bladder emptying is unaffected

why: **Overflow incontinence with a large residual after starting a first-generation antihistamine** = **diphenhydramine**. Its **antimuscarinic effect** relaxes the detrusor, causing retention, especially in older men.

drug.name: Diphenhydramine
drug.how: Blocks H1 receptors; also antimuscarinic and sedating
drug.use: Allergy, insomnia (OTC), motion sickness, extrapyramidal reactions
drug.watch: Sedation, dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, confusion in the elderly, blurred vision

stem: A 38-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has had her pyridostigmine dose doubled over the past week for increasing weakness. She now has abdominal cramps, watery diarrhea, drooling, and diffuse muscle weakness with twitching. Heart rate is 46/min, pupils are 2 mm, and bowel sounds are hyperactive. Ptosis is no worse than before.
oneliner: 38F + myasthenia on pyridostigmine, dose doubled + cramps, diarrhea, drooling + weakness with twitching + HR 46, pupils 2 mm + hyperactive bowel sounds → what is going on?
ask: Which of the following best explains her condition?

whyNot.A: **Myasthenic crisis**: weakness without bradycardia, miosis, drooling or diarrhea
whyNot.B: **Steroid myopathy**: proximal weakness without autonomic signs; she takes no steroid
whyNot.C: **Botulism**: dilated pupils, dry mouth and descending paralysis, not drooling and cramps
whyNot.E: **Lambert-Eaton**: dry mouth, hyporeflexia, improves with exercise; no cholinergic excess

answer: Cholinergic crisis (excess acetylcholine; atropine treats the muscarinic signs)
why: **Bradycardia, miosis, drooling, cramps, diarrhea and fasciculations after raising a cholinesterase inhibitor** = **cholinergic crisis**: excess acetylcholine at muscarinic (SLUDGE) and nicotinic (twitching, weakness) receptors.

drug.name: Pyridostigmine
drug.how: Blocks acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
drug.use: Myasthenia gravis, reversal of neuromuscular block (neostigmine)
drug.watch: Cholinergic crisis: SLUDGE, bradycardia, miosis, fasciculations, weakness; treat with atropine

stem: A 29-year-old woman with epilepsy has been seizure-free for 2 years on phenytoin. She began taking an over-the-counter acid reducer for heartburn 8 days ago. She now has double vision and a wide-based, unsteady gait, and horizontal nystagmus is seen on gaze to either side. Her phenytoin level is 38 µg/mL (therapeutic 10 to 20).
oneliner: 29F + epilepsy on stable phenytoin + new heartburn pill 8 d ago + diplopia, ataxia, nystagmus + phenytoin 38 → what interaction?
ask: Which of the following mechanisms best explains the rise in phenytoin level?

options.C: Inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 metabolism

whyNot.A: **Displacement**: causes only a brief rise in free drug, not a sustained rise in total level
whyNot.B: **Renal excretion**: phenytoin is cleared by hepatic metabolism, not the kidney
whyNot.D: **Larger Vd**: would **lower** the plasma level

answer: Cimetidine inhibits CYP450 metabolism of phenytoin
why: **Phenytoin toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia) after starting a heartburn drug** = **cimetidine**, a **CYP450 inhibitor**. Phenytoin metabolism is slowed, so its level climbs.

drug.name: Cimetidine
drug.how: Blocks H2 receptors; inhibits CYP450 enzymes and androgen binding
drug.watch: CYP inhibition (phenytoin, warfarin, theophylline), gynecomastia, confusion, reduces renal creatinine secretion

stem: A 6-year-old boy develops jaw and generalized muscle rigidity, a core temperature of 40.4 C and a heart rate of 160/min shortly after induction of anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine for a hernia repair. Blood tests show potassium of 6.4 mEq/L and a rising creatine kinase. His father had a similar reaction during surgery as a young man. The boy has had no muscle symptoms with exercise.
oneliner: 6M + rigidity, 40.4 C, tachycardia after sevoflurane + succinylcholine + K 6.4, rising CK + father had same reaction → underlying defect?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?

options.E: Abnormal ryanodine receptor causing uncontrolled calcium release

whyNot.A: **CPT deficiency**: causes exercise or fasting myoglobinuria, and he has no exercise symptoms
whyNot.B: **Phosphorylase kinase deficiency**: a glycogen storage disease with exercise-related symptoms and no anesthetic trigger
whyNot.C: **Na-K ATPase defect**: not an anesthetic-triggered, dominantly inherited hypermetabolic crisis
whyNot.D: **Mitochondrial ATP synthase defect**: would cause lactic acidosis and chronic symptoms, not a trigger-linked crisis with a family history of the same event

why: **Rigidity + hyperthermia + hyperkalemia within minutes of a volatile agent plus succinylcholine, with an affected father** = malignant hyperthermia. A dominant **ryanodine receptor (RYR1) variant** lets calcium pour out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, causing sustained contraction and heat.

drug.name: Volatile anesthetics + succinylcholine
drug.class: Inhaled anesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane) and depolarizing neuromuscular blocker
drug.how: Trigger Ca2+ release through abnormal ryanodine receptor in susceptible patients
drug.watch: Malignant hyperthermia: rigidity, fever, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; treat with dantrolene

stem: A 10-year-old boy undergoes an appendectomy under rapid-sequence induction with a short-acting depolarizing muscle relaxant. Three hours later in recovery he is awake, opens his eyes and follows commands by blinking, but he cannot breathe on his own or move his limbs. His temperature is normal, his muscles are flaccid, and no sedatives remain in his system.
oneliner: 10M + appendectomy with short-acting depolarizing relaxant + 3 h later awake, blinks to command + apneic, flaccid + normal temperature → which enzyme is deficient?
ask: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes best explains this finding?

whyNot.A: **MAO**: breaks down catecholamines and serotonin; it does not clear succinylcholine
whyNot.B: **Tyrosine hydroxylase**: makes catecholamines; deficiency gives no prolonged paralysis after a relaxant
whyNot.C: **Junctional acetylcholinesterase**: clears ACh at the endplate; succinylcholine itself is destroyed by the plasma enzyme
whyNot.D: **ACE**: converts angiotensin I and degrades bradykinin; unrelated to relaxant clearance

why: **Awake but paralyzed for hours after a depolarizing relaxant** = prolonged succinylcholine block. The drug is normally cleared within minutes by **plasma cholinesterase**, so a deficient or atypical enzyme leaves the endplate depolarized.

drug.name: Succinylcholine
drug.how: Nicotinic ACh receptor agonist that causes persistent depolarization; broken down by plasma cholinesterase
drug.watch: Prolonged apnea in pseudocholinesterase deficiency; malignant hyperthermia; hyperkalemia

stem: A 10-month-old boy is brought in unresponsive after his father, treating diarrhea, gave him three adult doses of an over-the-counter antidiarrheal tablet crushed in juice. His respirations are 6/min and shallow, his abdomen is distended, and his pupils are pinpoint. Glucose is normal.
oneliner: 10M + diarrhea treated by father with 3 adult doses of OTC antidiarrheal + unresponsive, RR 6, pinpoint pupils, distended abdomen → best antidote?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to give now?

whyNot.A: **Physostigmine**: antidote for anticholinergic poisoning, which would cause dilated pupils
whyNot.B: **Bethanechol**: a muscarinic agonist that would worsen abdominal symptoms, not reverse respiratory depression
whyNot.C: **Epinephrine**: for anaphylaxis or cardiac arrest, no role against opioid-induced hypoventilation
whyNot.D: **Diphenhydramine**: an antihistamine that adds sedation and does not reverse respiratory depression

why: **Slow respirations + pinpoint pupils + ileus after an antidiarrheal overdose** = opioid toxicity from **loperamide**, an opioid agonist that works in the gut but reaches the CNS in overdose and in infants. **Naloxone** competitively blocks the mu receptor.

drug.name: Loperamide
drug.how: Mu agonist in gut wall slows motility; P-glycoprotein normally keeps it out of the CNS
drug.watch: Constipation, ileus; CNS opioid toxicity in infants or overdose (reverse with naloxone); QT prolongation in large doses

stem: An 82-year-old woman received intravenous morphine by patient-controlled analgesia for 3 days after hip surgery. She is now difficult to arouse, with a respiratory rate of 6/min and pinpoint pupils. Her serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL, up from a baseline of 0.9, and she has taken no other sedatives. The dose on the pump has not changed.
oneliner: 82F + IV morphine PCA 3 d after hip surgery + RR 6, pinpoint pupils + creatinine 1.8 (baseline 0.9) + dose unchanged → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains her respiratory depression?

options.A: Accumulation of an active metabolite that is cleared by the kidney

whyNot.B: **Autoinhibition of metabolism**: would raise the parent drug; this is not a recognized morphine effect
whyNot.C: **Tolerance**: causes less respiratory depression over days, not more
whyNot.D: **Receptor downregulation**: also reduces the effect
whyNot.E: **Bioavailability**: morphine is given intravenously, which is 100% bioavailable

answer: Accumulation of morphine-6-glucuronide in renal impairment
why: **Unchanged IV dose + falling creatinine clearance + new respiratory depression** = accumulation of **morphine-6-glucuronide**, an active metabolite cleared by the kidney. Reduce the dose or switch to an opioid without active renal metabolites.

drug.name: Morphine
drug.how: Mu agonist; hepatic glucuronidation to active M6G, cleared by the kidney
drug.watch: Respiratory depression, miosis, constipation; metabolite builds up in renal failure

stem: A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, taking amlodipine and metformin, has had an uncomplicated hernia repair. He is given scheduled intravenous ketorolac for pain. On postoperative day 2 his urine output falls to 200 mL/day and his creatinine rises from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL. His blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg, urinalysis shows no cells or casts, and his bladder scan is empty.
oneliner: 74M + diabetes, hypertension, amlodipine + IV ketorolac after hernia repair + oliguria, creatinine 1.1 to 2.4 + BP 142/84, bland urine, empty bladder → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains his kidney injury?

options.A: Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilation
options.C: Direct tubular toxicity by an opioid metabolite
options.E: Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli

whyNot.B: **Efferent dilation**: would lower filtration pressure only with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and he takes neither; NSAIDs act on the afferent side
whyNot.C: **Opioid metabolite toxicity**: no opioid was given
whyNot.D: **Bladder outlet obstruction**: bladder scan is empty
whyNot.E: **Immune complex disease**: bland urine with no cells or casts

why: **Oliguria + creatinine rise on an NSAID in a diabetic hypertensive patient** = hemodynamic AKI. NSAIDs block COX, so **renal prostaglandins fall, the afferent arteriole constricts** and GFR drops.

drug.name: Ketorolac
drug.how: Blocks prostaglandin synthesis, removing afferent arteriolar vasodilation
drug.use: Short-term moderate to severe postoperative pain
drug.watch: Acute kidney injury, GI bleeding, bleeding risk; avoid in renal impairment

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought in 2 days after swallowing about 100 tablets of an over-the-counter pain reliever after an argument. She vomited at first, then felt well for a day. Now she has right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. AST is 6,200 U/L, bilirubin is 5 mg/dL and INR is 3.8. She has no tinnitus, her respiratory rate is 14/min and her arterial pH is normal.
oneliner: 19F + ~100 OTC analgesic tablets 2 d ago + well for 1 d, then RUQ pain, jaundice + AST 6,200, INR 3.8 + no tinnitus, RR 14 → mechanism of liver injury?
ask: Which of the following best explains the liver injury?

options.C: Depletion of glutathione, allowing a toxic metabolite to bind hepatocyte proteins
options.E: Immune hapten formation against a halogenated metabolite

whyNot.A: **Superoxide formation by NADPH oxidase**: part of phagocyte killing; not the cause of this hepatocyte necrosis
whyNot.B: **Inhibition of beta-oxidation**: causes microvesicular steatosis (valproate, tetracycline), not acute massive necrosis after a single dose
whyNot.D: **Canalicular blockade**: would cause cholestasis with a high alkaline phosphatase, not AST in the thousands

why: **Single large ingestion, a symptom-free interval, then fulminant hepatitis with a normal respiratory rate and no tinnitus** = acetaminophen toxicity (not aspirin). CYP2E1 makes **NAPQI**; when **glutathione runs out** NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins and causes centrilobular necrosis. Treat with N-acetylcysteine.

drug.name: Acetaminophen
drug.how: Overdose saturates glucuronidation and sulfation; CYP2E1 makes toxic NAPQI, cleared by glutathione
drug.watch: Centrilobular hepatic necrosis; antidote is N-acetylcysteine (replenishes glutathione)

stem: A 45-year-old woman who drinks three to four glasses of wine every day has taken an over-the-counter pain reliever at a dose of 5 g/day for 5 days for back pain. She now has nausea and right upper quadrant discomfort. AST is 1,400 U/L and ALT is 1,100 U/L. She has no rash or fever, and hepatitis serologies are negative.
oneliner: 45F + daily wine + OTC pain reliever 5 g/day x 5 d + nausea, RUQ discomfort + AST 1,400, ALT 1,100 + no rash, negative hepatitis serologies → why the injury?
ask: Which of the following best explains why her liver was injured at this dose?

options.A: Induction of CYP2E1, increasing production of a toxic metabolite

whyNot.B: **More glucuronidation**: would shunt drug to a safe product and be protective
whyNot.C: **More sulfation**: also a safe route; would be protective
whyNot.D: **More glutathione**: would neutralize the toxic metabolite; chronic alcohol use lowers it
whyNot.E: **IgE-mediated degranulation**: would cause urticaria or anaphylaxis, and she has no rash

answer: CYP2E1 induction increases NAPQI formation (alcohol plus acetaminophen)
why: **Chronic alcohol + high-dose acetaminophen + hepatitis with negative serologies** = acetaminophen hepatotoxicity at a lower threshold. Alcohol **induces CYP2E1**, so more drug becomes **NAPQI**, and glutathione stores are also lower in people who drink.

drug.name: Acetaminophen
drug.how: Hepatic CYP2E1 converts a fraction to NAPQI, which glutathione normally neutralizes
drug.watch: Hepatotoxicity, worse with chronic alcohol use or fasting; antidote is N-acetylcysteine

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought in after taking about 100 aspirin tablets. She has tinnitus, vomiting and a respiratory rate of 32/min with a temperature of 38.3 C. Laboratory results: Na 140, Cl 100, HCO3 14 mEq/L; arterial pH 7.47 and PaCO2 20 mm Hg.
oneliner: 19F + ~100 aspirin tablets + tinnitus, vomiting, RR 32 + pH 7.47, PaCO2 20, HCO3 14, anion gap 26 → acid-base disorder?
ask: Which of the following acid-base disturbances does she have?

options.D: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and anion-gap metabolic acidosis
options.E: Anion-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation only

whyNot.A: **Respiratory acidosis alone**: PaCO2 is low, not high
whyNot.B: **Metabolic alkalosis alone**: HCO3 is low, not high
whyNot.C: **Normal**: pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 are all abnormal
whyNot.E: **Compensation only**: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, but hers is **20**, so there is an additional primary respiratory alkalosis

answer: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and anion-gap metabolic acidosis (salicylate)
why: **Tinnitus + tachypnea + fever after aspirin** = salicylate toxicity. Salicylate **stimulates the medullary respiratory center** (respiratory alkalosis) and **uncouples oxidative phosphorylation** (lactate and ketones, anion-gap acidosis); PaCO2 is lower than Winter's formula predicts.

drug.name: Aspirin (salicylate)
drug.how: In overdose stimulates the respiratory center and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation
drug.use: Pain, fever, antiplatelet effect, Kawasaki disease
drug.watch: Tinnitus, hyperthermia, mixed alkalosis and anion-gap acidosis; treat with bicarbonate and dialysis in severe cases

stem: A 44-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought in after drinking windshield washer fluid because liquor was unavailable. He has blurred vision described as a snowstorm, abdominal pain and deep rapid breathing. Arterial pH is 7.25, the anion gap is 24 and the serum osmolar gap is increased. Urine ketones are negative and urine microscopy shows no crystals.
oneliner: 44M + alcohol use disorder + drank windshield washer fluid + snowstorm vision, abdominal pain, deep breathing + pH 7.25, gap 24, osm gap up + no ketones, no crystals → toxic metabolite?
ask: Which of the following metabolites is responsible for his visual symptoms?

whyNot.A: **Acetaldehyde**: produced from ethanol, causes flushing and hangover, not optic injury
whyNot.B: **Acetic acid**: harmless end product of ethanol
whyNot.D: **Lactic acid**: explains part of the gap but does not damage the optic nerve
whyNot.E: **Oxalic acid**: from ethylene glycol; causes calcium oxalate crystals and kidney injury, absent here

why: **Windshield washer fluid + visual changes + high anion gap and osmolar gap** = methanol poisoning. **Alcohol dehydrogenase** converts methanol to formaldehyde and then **formic acid**, which injures the optic nerve and causes the acidosis.

drug.name: Methanol
drug.how: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to formaldehyde, then formic acid
drug.use: Solvent, windshield washer fluid, paint thinner
drug.watch: Optic nerve damage, anion-gap acidosis; treat with fomepizole, dialysis

chain: optic nerve injury, anion gap acidosis

stem: A 52-year-old dry-cleaning worker swallowed about 100 mL of carbon tetrachloride, mistaking it for a bottle of water, 36 hours ago. He now has nausea, right upper quadrant pain and dark urine. He is jaundiced, AST is 3,400 U/L and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. His electrocardiogram and neurologic examination are normal.
oneliner: 52M + dry-cleaning worker + swallowed ~100 mL carbon tetrachloride 36 h ago + jaundice, AST 3,400 + normal creatinine, ECG, neuro exam → mechanism of injury?
ask: Which of the following best explains his liver injury?

options.A: Glutathione depletion with accumulation of NAPQI
options.C: Immune hapten formation against a metabolite
options.E: Free radical formation with peroxidation of hepatocyte membrane lipids

whyNot.A: **Glutathione depletion / NAPQI**: the mechanism of acetaminophen, not a solvent
whyNot.B: **Beta-oxidation inhibition**: causes microvesicular steatosis, not massive necrosis within days
whyNot.C: **Immune hapten**: halothane-type hepatitis follows repeated exposure to a drug, with fever and eosinophilia
whyNot.D: **Cholestasis**: would show high alkaline phosphatase, not AST in the thousands

answer: Free radicals causing lipid peroxidation (carbon tetrachloride)
why: **Solvent ingestion + centrilobular necrosis within days** = carbon tetrachloride. CYP450 converts it to the **trichloromethyl free radical**, which attacks **membrane lipids** and impairs lipoprotein export, causing necrosis and fatty change.

drug.name: Carbon tetrachloride
drug.how: Converted by CYP450 to CCl3 free radicals that peroxidize membrane lipids
drug.use: Industrial solvent (past use in dry cleaning)
drug.watch: Centrilobular hepatic necrosis, fatty liver, renal injury

stem: A 34-year-old woman is one of 14 office workers who arrived early, within an hour after the building's ventilation system was treated with an unknown chemical overnight. All develop wheezing, drooling, tearing, vomiting, watery diarrhea and muscle twitching. Examination shows small pupils, heart rates of 50/min and copious airway secretions. Two have died. No one has fever, and bacterial and viral tests are pending.
oneliner: 34F + 14 office workers ill within 1 h of ventilation system chemical treatment + wheeze, drooling, tearing, vomiting, diarrhea, twitching + small pupils, HR 50 + 2 deaths + no fever → what exposure?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **Anthrax**: causes mediastinitis and fever over days, not secretions and small pupils within an hour
whyNot.B: **Botulinum toxin**: causes dry mouth, dilated pupils and descending paralysis
whyNot.C: **Staph enterotoxin**: causes vomiting within hours but not bronchorrhea, miosis and twitching
whyNot.D: **Viral gastroenteritis**: fever, and no secretions or fasciculations; not within an hour

why: **Sudden cholinergic syndrome (salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, diarrhea, small pupils, bradycardia, fasciculations) after a chemical treatment** = organophosphate poisoning. They **inhibit acetylcholinesterase**, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic and nicotinic synapses.

drug.name: Organophosphates
drug.how: Phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase so ACh accumulates
drug.use: Insecticides (parathion, malathion); nerve agents such as sarin
drug.watch: Cholinergic crisis: DUMBELS; treat with atropine and pralidoxime

stem: A 19-month-old girl is found by her mother holding an empty bottle of the mother's prenatal iron tablets. Over several hours she vomits blood and has bloody diarrhea, appears pale and lethargic, then seems better for a day. She then develops jaundice and liver failure and dies. Autopsy shows extensive hepatocyte necrosis.
oneliner: 19-month-old girl + empty bottle of mother's iron tablets + hematemesis, bloody diarrhea, lethargy + brief improvement + liver failure and death → mechanism of liver injury?
ask: Which of the following best explains the hepatic injury?

options.A: Free radical formation with peroxidation of membrane lipids

whyNot.B: **Activation of glutathione peroxidase**: would protect against oxidative damage
whyNot.C: **Inhibition of glutathione-S-transferase**: not the iron mechanism
whyNot.D: **DNA peroxidation**: lipids, not DNA, are the main target
whyNot.E: **Beta-oxidation inhibition**: causes microvesicular steatosis rather than massive necrosis after a corrosive ingestion

why: **Iron tablets + hematemesis, a latent phase, then liver failure** = iron poisoning. Free iron catalyzes **Fenton reactions** producing free radicals that **peroxidize membrane lipids** in hepatocytes and mitochondria.

drug.name: Ferrous sulfate
drug.how: Free iron generates hydroxyl radicals (Fenton reaction) and damages membranes
drug.watch: Hemorrhagic gastritis, anion-gap acidosis, hepatic failure; antidote is deferoxamine

stem: Healthy volunteers breathe rising CO2 concentrations while their alveolar ventilation is measured, first awake and then during anesthesia with halothane at 1.8 MAC. Ventilation is plotted against arterial PaCO2 for each condition.
oneliner: Volunteers + ventilation vs PaCO2 curve, awake vs halothane 1.8 MAC → how does the curve change?
ask: Compared with the awake curve, how does the anesthetized curve change?

options.A: Shifted right with a flatter slope
options.B: Shifted left with a steeper slope
options.C: Same position with a steeper slope
options.D: Shifted left with the same slope

whyNot.B: **Would mean more sensitivity to CO2**; anesthetics blunt the response
whyNot.C: **Steeper slope** means a stronger response to CO2; halothane weakens it
whyNot.D: **Leftward shift** means breathing starts at a lower PaCO2; opposite of depression
whyNot.E: **Volatile anesthetics** depress medullary chemoreceptor drive, so the curve changes

answer: Shifted right with a flatter slope (blunted ventilatory response to CO2)
why: **Volatile anesthetic at a high dose** depresses the medullary response to CO2: higher PaCO2 is needed to start breathing (**right shift**) and each rise in PaCO2 adds less ventilation (**flatter slope**).

drug.name: Halothane
drug.how: Dose-dependent CNS depression, including the medullary chemoreceptor response to CO2
drug.watch: Halothane hepatitis, malignant hyperthermia, myocardial sensitization to catecholamines, respiratory depression

chain: Higher PaCO2 needed to drive breathing

stem: A 48-year-old woman has taken weekly methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis for six years. Her joint symptoms are well controlled. Routine blood tests show alanine aminotransferase twice the upper limit of normal, with mild macrocytosis. She drinks little alcohol, and has no new cough or rash.
oneliner: 48F + rheumatoid arthritis + 6 years of weekly methotrexate + ALT twice normal + mild macrocytosis → which adverse effect belongs to the drug?
ask: Which adverse effect is most characteristic of her medication?

options.C: Retinopathy with loss of central vision

whyNot.A: That is a **glucocorticoid** effect, not methotrexate
whyNot.B: Seen with **penicillamine and gold**, not methotrexate
whyNot.D: Caused by **diuretics and aspirin**; methotrexate is not a typical cause

why: **Methotrexate** inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and causes **hepatotoxicity (fibrosis, cirrhosis)**, marrow suppression with macrocytosis, **pneumonitis**, and mucositis. Folate supplements reduce toxicity, and liver tests are monitored.

drug.name: Methotrexate
drug.how: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing purine and thymidylate synthesis and DNA replication
drug.use: Rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, leukemia, choriocarcinoma, ectopic pregnancy
drug.watch: Hepatic fibrosis, myelosuppression, pneumonitis, mucositis; teratogenic

idea.rule: Methotrexate toxicity follows the rapidly dividing cells and the liver.
also: Rescue with leucovorin; folate daily helps

stem: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes an older oral hypoglycemic drug from the first generation of its class. Fifteen minutes after drinking wine at dinner he has facial flushing, throbbing headache, palpitations and vomiting. He takes no antibiotics and has never been prescribed disulfiram.
oneliner: 55M + type 2 diabetes on first-generation oral hypoglycemic + flushing, headache, vomiting 15 min after wine → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused this reaction?

whyNot.A: A **biguanide**, not a first-generation drug; it causes GI upset and lactic acidosis but **no flushing reaction**
whyNot.B: A **second-generation** sulfonylurea; it does **not block aldehyde dehydrogenase**
whyNot.C: A **thiazolidinedione** that causes fluid retention and weight gain; no **alcohol flushing reaction**
whyNot.D: A **second-generation** sulfonylurea; it causes hypoglycemia but **no disulfiram-like reaction**

why: **First-generation sulfonylureas** such as chlorpropamide inhibit **aldehyde dehydrogenase**, so alcohol produces **acetaldehyde buildup** with flushing, headache and vomiting, the same as with disulfiram.

drug.name: Chlorpropamide
drug.how: Closes pancreatic beta-cell K-ATP channels to release insulin; also inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase
drug.watch: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, prolonged hypoglycemia, SIADH-like hyponatremia, weight gain

idea.rule: Drugs that block aldehyde dehydrogenase cause acetaldehyde buildup and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
also: Cefotetan and cefoperazone (cephalosporins with a methylthiotetrazole side chain)

stem: A 45-year-old man taking fluoxetine for depression is started on an oral antibiotic for a skin abscess grown as MRSA. Two days later he has agitation, sweating, diarrhea and a temperature of 39.4 C (103 F). Examination shows tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible ankle clonus. Muscle tone is increased mostly in the legs.
oneliner: 45M + fluoxetine + new oral MRSA antibiotic + agitation, diarrhea, fever + hyperreflexia + inducible clonus → which added drug?
ask: Which added drug most likely triggered this syndrome?

whyNot.A: Oral MRSA option with **no serotonergic** or MAO-inhibiting effect; causes photosensitivity
whyNot.B: Oral MRSA option that causes hyperkalemia and rash, with **no serotonergic** effect
whyNot.D: Oral MRSA option linked to **C. difficile** colitis, with **no serotonergic** effect
whyNot.E: Never used alone for MRSA; it **induces CYP450**, which would lower fluoxetine levels rather than add serotonin

why: **Linezolid** is a weak, reversible **MAO inhibitor**. Added to an **SSRI** it raises synaptic serotonin and produces **serotonin syndrome**: **hyperreflexia, inducible clonus, hyperthermia and diarrhea**. The other oral MRSA drugs have no serotonergic effect.

drug.name: Linezolid
drug.how: Binds the 50S subunit and blocks formation of the 70S initiation complex; also a weak reversible MAO inhibitor
drug.watch: Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia), peripheral and optic neuropathy

idea.rule: Serotonin syndrome follows adding another serotonergic drug to an SSRI.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is chased by a security guard after being seen inhaling fumes from a bag of glue. He collapses within a minute and is found pulseless. Crusted red lesions surround his nose and mouth and his clothing smells of solvent. Resuscitation fails. He had no convulsions and no sign of head trauma.
oneliner: 15M + inhaling glue from a bag + chased, collapses within 1 min, pulseless + perinasal crusted rash + no convulsions or head trauma → mechanism of death?
ask: Which mechanism most likely caused his death?

options.A: Medullary respiratory depression from profound CNS suppression
options.C: Intracranial hemorrhage from an acute hypertensive surge
options.D: Acute hepatic failure from solvent toxicity
options.E: Generalized seizure progressing to status epilepticus

whyNot.A: Possible in deep intoxication, but collapse **within a minute during exertion** with a sudden **pulseless** state points to the heart
whyNot.C: There is **no head trauma**, and a bleed would not make him **pulseless within a minute**
whyNot.D: Takes **days of repeated exposure** to develop, not death within a minute
whyNot.E: He had **no convulsions**, and a seizure does not cause abrupt **pulselessness**

why: Volatile solvents such as **toluene** **sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines**. Exertion or fright adds an adrenaline surge, triggering a **fatal ventricular arrhythmia** (sudden sniffing death). A **perinasal rash** is the typical sign of glue sniffing.

drug.name: Toluene (glue and paint inhalant)
drug.how: CNS depressant that sensitizes the myocardium to catecholamines
drug.use: No therapeutic use; abused by inhalation (glue, spray paint, thinner)
drug.watch: Sudden sniffing death from arrhythmia, renal tubular acidosis, leukoencephalopathy, hepatotoxicity, perinasal rash

idea.rule: Inhalant deaths are usually sudden arrhythmias, not slow organ failure.
also: Halothane and similar hydrocarbons sensitize the heart
Toluene: renal tubular acidosis and white matter disease

stem: A 35-year-old woman takes a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder. She is passing 5 liters of urine daily and is constantly thirsty. Urine osmolality is 120 mOsm/kg before and 125 after desmopressin. She also has a fine hand tremor and a TSH of 9.8 mU/L.
oneliner: 35F + bipolar disorder on mood stabilizer + polyuria, thirst + urine osm 120 → 125 after desmopressin + tremor + TSH 9.8 → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.B: Causes **tremor, hepatotoxicity and neural tube defects**; it does not cause **ADH resistance** or hypothyroidism
whyNot.C: Causes **SIADH (low sodium)**, the opposite of dilute urine, along with **agranulocytosis**
whyNot.D: An antipsychotic that causes **weight gain and sedation**; it does not cause **ADH resistance** or hypothyroidism
whyNot.E: Causes **Stevens-Johnson syndrome**, not polyuria or hypothyroidism

why: **Lithium** blocks the collecting duct's response to ADH, causing **nephrogenic diabetes insipidus** that does **not respond to desmopressin**. It also causes **tremor and hypothyroidism**.

drug.name: Lithium
drug.how: Inhibits inositol monophosphatase and GSK-3; exact mechanism unclear
drug.watch: Nephrogenic DI, tremor, hypothyroidism, Ebstein anomaly, narrow therapeutic index; levels rise with thiazides, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, dehydration

also: Levels rise with thiazides, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs
